title: How Long, O LORD? The Rise of the Chaldeans
summary: Habakkuk cries out to God about the violence and injustice he sees, complaining that the law is paralyzed and God seems not to listen. God answers that he is raising up the Chaldeans, a ruthless and swift nation, to judge Judah. Troubled, Habakkuk asks a second question: how can a God too pure to look on evil use a nation more wicked than those it swallows, a fisherman who hauls up people in his net and worships the net itself?
story: The prophets before Habakkuk warned Israel and Judah that judgment would come, and Nahum announced the end of Assyria, the empire that had terrorized the region. Habakkuk opens at a new moment. Assyria is falling or gone, and a new power, Babylon, is rising. Inside Judah, justice has broken down. The chapter's two complaints set up the problem the whole book will wrestle with. The first asks why God tolerates evil among his people; the answer, that he will send Babylon, raises the second, why he would use a worse evil to punish a lesser one. Chapter 2 will give God's reply, and chapter 3 the prophet's response of trust.
historical:
The Chaldeans were originally tribes in southern Mesopotamia near the Persian Gulf. In the late seventh century BC a Chaldean leader, Nabopolassar, seized Babylon (626 BC) and founded what historians call the Neo-Babylonian empire. Allied with the Medes, Babylon destroyed Nineveh in 612 BC, and under Nabopolassar's son Nebuchadnezzar it defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC and became master of the region, including Judah. Habakkuk 1 describes that rise from the perspective of one who has not yet felt its full weight: God says he is doing a work that people would not believe, which fits a time before Babylon's dominance was obvious.

The injustice of verses 2 to 4 fits Judah after the death of King Josiah in 609 BC. His son Jehoiakim reversed much of his father's reform, and Jeremiah condemned him for building his palace by unrighteousness and shedding innocent blood (Jeremiah 22:13-17). Many scholars therefore date the chapter to Jehoiakim's reign. Some place it slightly earlier, and a few read the wicked of verse 4 as a foreign oppressor rather than corrupt Judeans, though most take the first complaint as directed at Judah itself.
cultural:
The first complaint uses the language of Israel's law courts. The law (torah, God's instruction) is paralyzed, or numb, and justice never goes forth, because the courts that should protect the righteous are surrounded and bent by the wicked. For Habakkuk's audience, justice was not an abstraction but the daily business of elders and judges at the city gate. The description of the Babylonians draws on familiar images of terror: horses faster than leopards, fiercer than wolves hunting at evening, a vulture swooping on its prey, and siege ramps heaped up against fortress walls, a standard technique of Mesopotamian warfare.

The fishing image in verses 14 to 17 draws on a well known practice. Hooks, dragnets, and casting nets were used on the Nile and in the rivers and marshes of Mesopotamia, and Mesopotamian art sometimes pictured gods or kings catching enemies in a net. Habakkuk turns the image into an accusation: the conqueror treats human beings like fish with no ruler to protect them. Burning incense and offering sacrifice to the net is a pointed picture of a nation that worships its own instruments of power, making its military strength its god, as verse 11 says outright.
literary: The chapter is a dialogue between the prophet and God. Habakkuk speaks in verses 2 to 4, using the lament form familiar from the Psalms: an address to God, the question how long, and a description of distress. God replies in verses 5 to 11, and the speech is framed by commands to look and be astounded. Habakkuk speaks again from verse 12 to the end of the chapter, and his second complaint continues into 2:1, where he takes his stand on the watchtower. The second complaint is built on a contrast between who God is (from everlasting, holy, the Rock, too pure to look on evil) and what God seems to be allowing. Verse 12 contains a line, We will not die, which Jewish scribal tradition lists among a small number of places where scribes are said to have altered an expression out of reverence for God; some scholars think the original read you will not die, addressed to God.

outline.t: First complaint: violence and paralyzed justice
God's answer: I am raising up the Chaldeans
Second complaint: how can the holy God tolerate this?
The conqueror as a fisherman who worships his net

doctrines.note: God says I am raising up the Chaldeans. He governs the rise of nations and can use even a violent empire to accomplish his judgment, without approving its violence. The chapter asserts this sovereignty and lets the prophet voice how troubling it is.
Habakkuk's prayers are complaints, even protests, yet they are addressed to God and grounded in who he is. The chapter shows that honest questions spoken to God are a form of faith, not its failure.

Habakkuk appeals to God as everlasting, holy, the Rock, and too pure to look upon evil. His problem arises precisely because he believes these things; a lesser view of God would leave no tension to resolve.
The Babylonians make their own strength their god and sacrifice to their nets. Idolatry here is not only worship of carved images but trust in one's own power and success.

words.note: Chamas, violence, used three times in the chapter. It covers physical brutality and also the abuse of power through injustice and fraud. Habakkuk cries out that violence fills Judah (verse 2), and God answers that the Chaldeans come bent on violence (verse 9). The same word will return in the woes of chapter 2.

Mishpat, justice. Habakkuk complains that justice never goes forth and is perverted (verse 4), and God says the Chaldeans derive their justice from themselves (verse 7), recognizing no law above their own will. The contrast between God's justice and human self-made justice runs through the book.

Kasdim, the Chaldeans. The name first described a people of southern Mesopotamia, and by Habakkuk's time it had become a name for the Babylonians whose Chaldean dynasty ruled the empire. In Daniel the same word also refers to a class of learned diviners.

Tsur, rock, used here as a title for God, O Rock. The image of God as a rock, stable, sheltering, and immovable, is common in Israel's songs (Deuteronomy 32:4, Psalm 18:2). Habakkuk clings to it at the moment when God's actions seem most unsettling.

christ: Paul quoted this chapter in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch, after proclaiming that God raised Jesus from the dead: “For I am doing a work in your days that you would never believe, even if someone told you” (Acts 13:41, following the Greek translation of Habakkuk 1:5). The work in Habakkuk's day was the unexpected rise of Babylon as God's instrument of judgment; the work in Paul's day was the even more unexpected act of God in raising a crucified man. Paul applies the prophet's warning about unbelief to those who hear the gospel and scoff. The chapter's larger question, how a holy God can deal with human evil, is one the New Testament answers at the cross, where God does not ignore evil or simply destroy evildoers, but bears judgment himself and so shows that he is both just and the one who justifies (Romans 3:26). That is a theological connection rather than a prediction in Habakkuk's text.

hard.q: How can God use a nation more wicked than Judah to punish Judah?
hard.a: This is Habakkuk's own question, and the book takes it seriously. Several answers are offered in Scripture. First, God's use of a nation does not mean he approves of it: Isaiah 10 describes Assyria as the rod of God's anger and then announces judgment on Assyria for its arrogance, and Habakkuk 2 does the same for Babylon. Second, the judgment on Judah was not arbitrary; the prophets had warned for generations that covenant unfaithfulness would bring exile. Third, God's governance of history works through free human agents, who remain responsible for their cruelty even when their actions serve a larger purpose. Some readers find these answers sufficient; others think the Bible leaves a remainder of mystery, which is why God's reply in chapter 2 calls for faith and patience rather than offering a full explanation. What the chapter refuses is the easy answer that God does not care or is not in control.

questions: Habakkuk begins with How long, O LORD? What questions have you wanted to ask God, and have you felt free to ask them?
God's answer to Habakkuk's first question made the problem harder, not easier. How do you respond when an answer to prayer raises new difficulties?
The Babylonians made their own strength their god and worshiped their nets. What tools of success or power are people tempted to trust in that way today?
